source.title: Hungry Hungry Hippos: Towards Language Modeling with State Space Models
source.authors: Tri Dao; Daniel Y. Fu; Khaled Kamal Saab; A. Thomas; A. Rudra; Christopher Ré

page_placements.theme: Induction-style recall and copying in non-attention and hybrid architectures

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates a synthetic induction-head language-modeling task in two-layer models, but reports task accuracy rather than identifying or testing the proposed attention-head mechanism.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Olsson et al.'s claim about the role of induction tasks in in-context learning; that cited finding is not a result of this study and is not recorded as a row. The study reports its own induction-task accuracies in Table 2.
record.test_reason: The study uses the synthetic Induction Head task as a benchmark to compare sequence-layer architectures and motivate H3. It reports only end-of-sequence task accuracy for 2-layer models. It does not identify heads, previous-token composition, training dynamics, or the share of in-context learning carried by induction heads. The attention score of 100.0 is a comparator for the authors' own layer, not a test of any version. The Appendix D.2 attention construction is an informal sketch, not an empirical result.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that existing SSMs (S4D, GSS) fail the synthetic induction and associative-recall tasks, while attention and H3 solve them. They argue this gap reflects missing recall and comparison abilities. They also report that H3 nearly matches Transformers on language modeling and that hybrid H3-attention models outperform them. They use the synthetics only as motivation for H3's design.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures task accuracy on synthetic languages, rather than analyzing induction-head circuits or measuring training-time phase changes as in the original sources.

fits_no_version.finding: On the 2-layer synthetic Induction Head task, H3 and attention score 100.0, while S4D scores 35.6 and Gated State Spaces 6.8 (chance 5.0). The study measures task accuracy, not heads.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether a 2-layer sequence architecture can solve the synthetic induction (copy-after-token) task depends on the layer type: attention and H3 solve it, while S4D and GSS fail.

record.problems: The induction-task result is task accuracy, not mechanistic evidence about attention heads or their formation. Table 2 does not state the metric's units or uncertainty; the synthetic-task evaluation uses 5000 training examples and 500 test examples from the same distribution.
record.rows_left_out: No separate associative-recall result was included because it is not the induction behavior named by these claim versions. Other reported language-modeling and few-shot metrics do not measure induction-head behavior or its mechanism.

untested.parts: Head identification, composition with a previous-token head, and the mechanism itself; only task accuracy is reported.
All of it: no training-time dynamics.
All of it: Olsson et al.'s claim is only cited.
All of it: no induction-head detection in any model.
All of it: SuperGLUE few-shot scores are not attributed to any mechanism.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T2/tests label and its V1 supports verdict are overturned. The induction task is used as an architecture benchmark (T4). No versions are tested, so no verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Tests accuracy on the synthetic induction-head task, not whether attention heads form by composing with a previous-token head or how they implement the behavior.
No training-time analysis of head formation, in-context-learning gains, or loss-curve bumps.
No test of the share of large-transformer in-context learning carried by induction heads.
No analysis of induction-behaving heads across model families, sizes, runs, architectures, or modalities.
No test of how data or training setup affects induction-head formation or persistence of in-context learning.
Few-shot benchmark performance is reported, but the study does not test which heads or mechanisms carry few-shot learning.
No analysis of stages or multiple transitions in induction-head formation.

relation.reason: The study uses induction-inspired tasks and the prior attention construction to develop H3. Appendix D.2 supplies a hand-specified attention construction, rather than evidence that the claimed circuit forms during training.

tranche.reason: The induction-inspired synthetics motivate and benchmark H3 against other architectures. Their performance does not measure any claim version's learned mechanism, formation dynamics, or contribution to in-context learning.

source_check.notes: The r5 note's suggestion of V1 support should be removed: the trained GPT-style models include MLPs and their heads are not analyzed. These rows record architecture benchmark performance, including the authors' own H3 method.

statements.correction: Table 2, Induction Head: H3 100.0; Attention 100.0; S4D 35.6; Gated State Spaces 6.8; Random 5.0. Two-layer trained models. Table 1: vocabulary size 20. Task performance measured; learned induction-head circuits not identified. Table 12 explicitly reports accuracy for a separate associative-recall evaluation.
statements.problem: All scores and the two-layer setting match. Table 2 does not explicitly name its metric or units; 5.0 is labeled Random, with its interpretation as chance inferred from the vocabulary size.
